request.system:
You review a blog article an online shop is about to publish. You did not write it. You see the shop, the topic and the search it targets, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), and the article. Sentences about products end with the facts they rest on in brackets; [G] marks a sentence the writer says is general knowledge.

Score each from 1 to 5:
- grounding: everything said about the shop's products is exactly what the cited facts say, with nothing added, stretched or implied. One product claim the facts do not support caps this at 2. No invented experience ("we tested", customer stories), statistics or studies.
- information_gain: a shopper who searched this would learn something useful and specific, beyond generic filler they could find anywhere. Padding, repetition and vague praise lower it.
- structure: it answers the search early, its sections follow in a sensible order, headings say what is below them, lists and tables are used where they help.
- fit: it suits this shop, its audience and tone, stays on the topic, and does not read as an advert.
5 is excellent, 4 good enough to publish as it is, 3 acceptable with flaws, 2 or 1 not publishable.

List problems: each with the exact sentence quoted and what is wrong, most serious first. Leave the list empty if there are none.

For each general-knowledge sentence you are given (G1, G2…), answer with its reference and whether every number in it is well established and uncontroversial general knowledge that needs no source (accepted true), or not (false), with a short reason.

<article>
Title: How to Make Cold Brew Coffee at Home: Beans, Grind, Ratio and Steep Time

To make cold brew coffee, steep coarsely ground coffee in cold water for many hours, then separate the grounds and dilute the concentrate to taste. Most recipes call for somewhere between 12 and 24 hours of steeping [G]. The variables that decide whether you get a smooth, chocolatey concentrate or a flat, bitter one are the beans, the grind, the ratio of coffee to water and the steep time. This guide covers each of them, then walks through the process step by step.

## What cold brew is and why it tastes different

Cold brew is an immersion method. Instead of water passing through a bed of coffee, as in pour-over, the grounds sit fully submerged in cold or room-temperature water for hours rather than minutes.

Temperature changes what ends up in the cup. Hot water extracts acids and aromatic compounds quickly, which is why a hot filter can taste bright and lively. Cold water extracts far more slowly and pulls out less of that bright acidity, so cold brew tends to taste rounder, smoother and less sharp.

This is also the difference between cold brew and iced coffee. Iced coffee is brewed hot and then chilled or poured over ice, so it keeps the acidity of a hot brew. Cold brew never sees hot water at all, which gives it its softer, heavier character.

You can make cold brew in almost any container, but a dedicated brewer makes the job tidier. Our [Cold Brew Jar](P1) is an immersion brewer made by Fernhill [F2, F3].

{{P1}}

## Choosing beans for cold brew

Cold brew mutes acidity and emphasises body and sweetness, so the coffee you pick shapes the result more than you might expect.

- **Medium roasts with chocolate and caramel character** are the classic, forgiving choice. They give a sweet, rounded concentrate that works well black or with milk.
- **Fruity light roasts** give a brighter, more unusual cup. Expect berry and floral notes rather than a straight chocolate profile.

For a dependable cold brew, our [Colombia Huila](P2) is a washed-process medium roast [F11, F20]. Its tasting notes are red apple, caramel and milk chocolate [F22]. It comes in 250 g and 1 kg sizes [F14].

{{P2}}

If you want something more adventurous, our [Ethiopia Guji, natural process](P4) is a light roast with tasting notes of blueberry, dark chocolate and jasmine [F41, F42]. It is available as whole bean, filter grind or espresso grind [F35].

Whichever coffee you choose, buy it as whole bean and grind it coarse yourself. A filter grind is too fine for a steep that lasts many hours and tends to turn the concentrate bitter and silty. You can browse the full range in our [coffee beans collection](L3).

## Grind coarse, like for French press

Grind size matters more in cold brew than in almost any other method, because the coffee is in contact with water for so long.

- **Too fine:** the grounds over-extract, the concentrate tastes bitter and harsh, and fine particles make it muddy and hard to filter.
- **Too coarse:** too little is extracted and the concentrate comes out thin and weak, even after a long steep.

Aim for a coarse grind, similar to what you would use for a French press: chunky particles roughly the texture of coarse sea salt. Consistency matters as much as the setting, since a burr grinder produces more even particles than a blade grinder.

Our [Hand Grinder](P3) has conical steel burrs and external click adjustment with 30 settings [F23, F26]. Its settings range from espresso to French press [F27]. It holds 25 g of beans [F28].

{{P3}}

With any grinder that has a small hopper, a large cold brew batch means grinding in several rounds. Set the grind once, leave it alone, and grind load after load into the same container so every particle comes from the same setting. If you brew big batches often, have a look at our [grinders collection](L2).

## How much coffee and how long to steep

Cold brew is usually made as a concentrate, which you then dilute when serving. As a general guide, a concentrate uses roughly 1:5 to 1:8 coffee to water by weight [G]. A ready-to-drink cold brew that needs no dilution sits closer to 1:12 to 1:15 [G].

Weigh both the coffee and the water rather than measuring by volume. Scoops of coarse coffee vary a lot in weight, and weighing is the only way to repeat a batch you liked or to change one thing at a time when you adjust.

With our Cold Brew Jar, the filter basket holds up to 150 g of coarse ground coffee [F6]. The jar has a capacity of 1.5 litre and makes 1.5 litres of concentrate [F1, F7]. The recommended steep time for the Cold Brew Jar is 12 to 18 hours in the fridge [F10].

Start in the middle of that steep window and adjust from there by taste. If the concentrate tastes thin or sour, steep longer or grind a touch finer. If it tastes bitter or woody, shorten the steep or grind coarser. Change only one variable per batch so you know what made the difference.

## Step by step with the Cold Brew Jar

Here is the full process from beans to concentrate.

- **Weigh and grind.** Weigh your beans and grind them coarse, in several rounds if your grinder has a small hopper.
- **Fill the basket.** Our Cold Brew Jar has a fine stainless steel filter basket, which holds up to 150 g of coarse ground coffee [F5, F6].
- **Add the water slowly.** Pour cold, filtered water in gradually so every ground gets wet. Dry pockets of coffee extract unevenly, so give it a gentle stir if any grounds float to the top.
- **Seal it.** Close the jar with its airtight lid [F8].
- **Refrigerate.** Put the jar in the fridge; it fits in a fridge door [F9].
- **Steep.** Leave it for the recommended 12 to 18 hours in the fridge [F10].
- **Remove the grounds.** Lift out the filter basket and let it drain over the jar before setting it aside.

The Cold Brew Jar is a glass jar [F4]. A clear vessel lets you check that all the grounds are saturated and see the colour of the brew as it steeps. Once the grounds are out, extraction stops, so remove them promptly when the time is up.

## Diluting, serving and storing your concentrate

A batch from our Cold Brew Jar is 1.5 litres of concentrate, not ready-to-drink coffee [F7]. A good starting point is to dilute concentrate 1:1 with water or milk over ice [G]. From there, adjust to taste: more water for a lighter, more refreshing glass, less for something closer to the strength of a hot brew.

Some ways to serve it:

- **Black over ice**, diluted with cold water.
- **With milk or a plant milk**, which suits chocolate and caramel-leaning coffees.
- **With tonic water**, poured over ice with the concentrate floated on top, for a bright, bitter-sweet long drink. Fruity light roasts work especially well here.

Keep the concentrate sealed and cold. The Cold Brew Jar has an airtight lid [F8]. Cold brew concentrate is generally best drunk within about a week to ten days, after which the flavour gradually flattens [G]. Dilute only what you plan to drink, since diluted cold brew loses its character faster than the concentrate.

## No dedicated jar? Use a French press

If you already own a French press, or you want one brewer that handles both hot coffee and cold brew, you can make a smaller batch in it. Our [French Press](P6) is an immersion brewer with a capacity of 1 litre [F52, F53]. It has a four-layer mesh filter [F58].

{{P6}}

The method is simple:

- Add coarse grounds to the empty beaker and pour in cold, filtered water, making sure all the coffee is wet.
- Rest the lid on top with the plunger pulled up, then cover and steep in the fridge.
- When the time is up, press the plunger down slowly.
- Pour all the concentrate off into a separate sealed bottle straight away.

That last step matters. A plunger only pushes the grounds to the bottom; the coffee is still in contact with them, so leaving it in the beaker means it keeps extracting and drifts towards bitterness. All parts of our French Press come apart for cleaning [F59].

For more brewers built around steeping rather than pouring, see our [immersion brewers collection](L4).

## The short version

Use a medium roast for a classic, chocolatey cold brew or a fruity light roast for something brighter. Grind coarse, as for a French press. Weigh your coffee and water, aiming for a concentrate ratio, and steep in the fridge before removing the grounds promptly. Dilute to taste when serving, keep the concentrate sealed and cold, and adjust one variable at a time until the batch tastes exactly how you want it.
</article>
